title: Hollow Pyramid Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: gap-row-edge per-cell checks versus classifying each row once and building its star region directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, print a centered pyramid with n rows where only the two slanted edges are stars and everything between them is a space, except the very last row, which forms a completely solid base.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a centered pyramid with n rows where only the two slanted edges are stars and everything between them is a space, except the very last row, which forms a completely solid base.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Tent With a Solid Groundsheet
blocks.text: Picture a triangular tent made only of its two slanted support poles, with open air between them, standing on a solid groundsheet at the bottom. The poles trace the outline of the triangle, hollow in the middle, while the base they are anchored to is completely filled in.

blocks.caption: Only the two slanted edges are stars, except the solid base row

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","    *","Width 2 times 1 minus 1 is 1, a single star with no interior at all, so there is nothing to hollow out."],["Row 2","   * *","Width 3, a star, one hollow space, a star, exactly the two edges of this row."],["Row 3","  *   *","Width 5, a star, three hollow spaces, a star, only the edges are filled."],["Row 4"," *     *","Width 7, a star, five hollow spaces, a star, still only the two slanted edges."],["Row 5","*********","This is row n, the base row, so the entire width 9 region is solid stars, not just its edges."]]}

blocks.text: With only 1 row, that single row is also the base row, so it is simply one solid star.
No rows at all, so nothing is printed.

The hollow square already showed that classifying rows into a small number of types beats checking every cell. This shape needs one more idea on top of that: spotting the row that does not follow the general rule at all.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The growing width formula here, 2i minus 1, is exactly the same odd, growing star count already seen in the full pyramid, only now each row is hollow instead of solid.

Observation 2: Testing a small example, n equal to 5, shows there are really three distinct row types, not two: the apex row, where the width is only 1 and there is no interior to hollow out; the ordinary hollow rows, where only the two edge positions are stars; and the base row, which is completely solid.

Observation 3: The base row is the one that breaks the hollow rule entirely, if it were treated like every other row, it would come out with hollow gaps instead of a solid foundation, so it needs to be spotted and special cased before any general formula is written.

Observation 4: Once every row is classified into one of these three types, each one can still be built directly, a single star, a star-gap-star, or a solid run, exactly the same construction technique used throughout this division.
Naming that exception, the solid base row, out loud before writing any code is what keeps the general hollow-edge logic clean instead of tangled with a special case buried inside it.

Use an outer loop for each row i, and an inner loop that checks every column this row uses, first checking whether the column is in the leading gap, then whether this is the last row, and finally whether the position sits on one of the two edges of the star region.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Compute the gap size, n minus i, and the star region width, 2i minus 1.
For each column, if it is still in the gap, print a space.
Otherwise, if this is the last row, print a star, the base is solid.
Otherwise, print a star only at the very first or very last position of the star region, and a space everywhere else in between.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check the gap, then the row type, then the edge position

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: gap and width are computed once per row, using the same shrinking-gap and odd-growing-width formulas from the full pyramid, before the inner loop even begins.
The check for i equal to n, the base row, is repeated for every single column in that row, even though it is a row level fact that never changes within the row.
The edge check, k equal to 0 or k equal to width minus 1, is also re-evaluated per column, even though only two specific positions in the whole row will ever satisfy it.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column position is checked against the gap, the row type, and the edge condition before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total width across all rows is proportional to n squared, and every position gets its own multi part check.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: the row type, whether this is the solid base or a hollow row above it, is already known before the row even starts, so there is no need to re-check it for every single column. The whole star region for a row can be built directly in one operation, either fully solid or just its two edges, without visiting each position individually.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the row-level fact, is this the base row, and the two edge positions get re-derived once per column, even though the row's type never changes within itself.

What stays the same as the hollow square: the underlying insight, classify the row once, then build it directly instead of checking cell by cell.

What is different here: there are three row types instead of two, an apex row with a single star and no interior, ordinary hollow rows with only their two edges filled, and one solid base row that is a genuine exception to the hollow rule.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, once a row's type is known, its exact content, a lone star, a star-gap-star, or a solid run, can be built in one or two operations.

The core idea: classify each row once as apex, hollow, or solid base, then build its star region directly, attach the leading gap, and print the row once.

For each row, decide once whether it is the solid base row or a hollow row above it. Build the star region directly, either a solid run of stars for the base, or a star, a gap of spaces, and a star for every other row, then attach the leading gap and print the whole row with one call.
For each row, decide once whether it is the solid base row, the single-star apex, or an ordinary hollow row, then build the star region directly, attach the leading gap, and print the row once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: decide the row type once, build the star region directly

blocks.text: This works because every row's type, apex, ordinary hollow, or solid base, is fully determined before the row is built, using only i and n; a direct repeat operation constructs a solid run in one step, and a star-gap-star construction handles every ordinary hollow row just as directly, with no dependence on checking individual columns. Special casing the width 1 apex and the i equal to n base row up front means the general star-gap-star construction never has to handle those two shapes incorrectly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["Row i is the apex, width equal to 1","It is built directly as a single star with no gap construction needed","The narrowest row is correct immediately, with no attempt to hollow out a non-existent interior"],["Row i is an ordinary hollow row, not the apex and not the base","It is built by concatenating a star, a width minus 2 space gap, and a star","The row is correct immediately, showing only its two slanted edges"],["Row i is the base row, i equal to n","It is built as a single repeat operation producing width stars, completely solid","The base is correct immediately, with no hollow gaps despite following the same width formula as the row above it"]]}

items: gap and width are computed once per row using the same shrinking-gap and odd-growing-width formulas from the full pyramid, then the row is classified using two simple checks, is it the base row, is its width only 1.
The base row is built with a single repeat operation producing width stars, exactly the same direct-construction technique used for solid rows throughout this division.
Every ordinary hollow row is built by concatenating a star, a gap of width minus 2 spaces, and a star, three pieces assembled once instead of checked position by position.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with a single row-type decision per row instead of a per cell check, and O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Build all 5 rows","\"    *\", \"   * *\", \"  *   *\", \" *     *\", \"*********\"","Each row is still built directly from its own classification, apex, hollow, or solid base, independent of the others."],["Join with newlines","All 5 rows joined into one string","Joining every row in advance assembles the complete hollow pyramid, with its solid base, as a single string before any output happens."],["Print once","The full pattern appears in one call","A single output call now produces the entire hollow pyramid, regardless of how many rows it has."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own classification and lengths, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete hollow pyramid, including its one solid base row, as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole shape, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: Hollow shapes with a solid base combine two ideas already seen separately: a row that is only its two edges, and a special final row that behaves completely differently from the rest. Spotting that special case up front, and handling it as its own row type, avoids tangled per cell logic entirely.

items: Forgetting that a width of 1 star has no interior to hollow out, and would otherwise produce an empty string instead of a single star.
Applying the hollow edge rule to the base row by mistake, when the base row should always be completely solid.
Getting the gap or width formula wrong, reusing the ones from a plain solid pyramid without adjusting for the hollow interior.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Produces an empty pattern with no output."],["n = 1","The single row is both the top and the solid base, so it is just one star."]]}

blocks.text: When a shape has one row that behaves differently from all the others, like this solid base, calling that out explicitly as a special case before writing the general row formula avoids a lot of tangled conditional logic later.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "does every row follow the same rule here", think: name the exception, the solid base row, explicitly before writing the general hollow-edge formula.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every cell", think: classify the row into apex, hollow, or solid base once, then build it directly.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

items: Why is it important to identify a row that breaks the general pattern before writing the main loop logic?
How would this approach change if the solid row needed to be the apex instead of the base?
Can you extend this same three-way row classification to a hollow diamond, which has both a widening and a narrowing half?
What is the total star count across the whole shape, and how much less is it than a fully solid full pyramid of the same size?
How would you adapt this to make the two hollow edges thicker, two stars wide instead of one?
The full pyramid, whose odd, growing width formula, 2i minus 1, is reused here unchanged, just applied to a hollow interior instead of a solid one.
The hollow square, whose row-classification insight, decide the type once, build directly, generalizes here to three row types instead of two.
The hollow diamond and butterfly patterns later in this division, which combine this same hollow-edge technique with a second, mirrored half.
Any shape with one row or column that behaves as a genuine exception, which should always be identified and special cased before the general formula is written.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: multi part per cell checks in the brute force version, one row-type decision per row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: hollow shape printing that combines the growing pyramid formula with a hollow interior, plus one row, the base, that breaks the hollow rule entirely and must be handled as its own special case.

Core Idea: classify each row as the apex, an ordinary hollow row, or the solid base, using i and n alone, then build that row's star region directly, either a single star, a star-gap-star, or a solid run, and join every row for a single output call.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: a shape can follow a general rule almost everywhere and still need one row treated as a genuine, explicit exception.

Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with enough conditionals; explicitly naming the three row types, especially the base exception, before coding is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: same width formula as the full pyramid, but hollow at the edges except the solid base row.
